lessons.title: Family Members and Relationships
lessons.content:
La famille is the centre of French Caribbean and French society, and family questions open almost every oral examination. Start with the core vocabulary: le père (father), la mère (mother), le frère (brother), la sœur (sister), les grands-parents (grandparents), l'oncle (uncle) and la tante (aunt). Note that French uses mon before a masculine noun, ma before a feminine noun and mes before a plural noun: mon frère, ma sœur, mes cousins. A family is described with the verb être: Ma famille est grande — my family is big.

Possessive adjectives must agree with the thing possessed, not with the owner. A girl says mon père (my father) and ma mère (my mother) exactly as a boy does. To give ages, French uses avoir (to have): J'ai seize ans, literally 'I have sixteen years'. Do not write 'Je suis seize ans', which is one of the most common errors in the examination. Marital status uses être: Mon oncle est marié; ma tante est célibataire.

For the oral and the written paper, prepare a short description of your own family: Nous sommes cinq à la maison — mon père, ma mère, mes deux sœurs et moi. Add one detail about each person using an adjective: Mon père est travailleur (hard-working); ma sœur est bavarde (talkative). In the francophone Caribbean, families are often extended, with cousins, godparents and grandparents living close by, so vocabulary such as mon demi-frère (half-brother), ma belle-mère (stepmother) and mon parrain (godfather) is useful too.
objectives: Name family members in French with the correct possessive adjective
Describe relationships between members of a family
Use avoir and être accurately in the present tense when talking about family
Compare the French extended family with your own family
concepts: Family vocabulary (le père, la mère, le frère, la sœur, les grands-parents)
Possessive adjectives (mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses)
Avoir for age (J'ai quinze ans) and être for descriptions
Marital status (marié(e), célibataire, divorcé(e))
Talking about a family photograph

experiment.description: Flashcard Trainer: flip cards to learn family vocabulary (père, mère, frère, sœur, grands-parents) and the possessive adjectives mon/ma/mes.

lessons.title: Describing People: Appearance and Character
lessons.content:
Describing people is a set task in both Paper 02 and the oral examination. Physical adjectives come mostly after the noun and must agree with it: un homme grand, une femme grande, des cheveux noirs, les yeux bleus. A few very common adjectives go before the noun — grand, petit, jeune, vieux, beau, joli, bon, mauvais — so we say un petit garçon and une vieille dame, not un garçon petit.

Character adjectives behave in the same way: Mon frère est très drôle (funny); ma cousine est timide mais très gentille. Note the feminine and plural forms: travailleur becomes travailleuse, and paresseux becomes paresseuse. The verb être is used for permanent descriptions, while avoir describes hair and eyes: Elle a les cheveux longs et frisés (She has long, curly hair).

Comparisons lift a description above the ordinary: Mon père est plus grand que ma mère; ma sœur est moins bavarde que moi; mon ami est aussi sportif que mon frère. For the examination, memorise a description of a person you know well — about five sentences covering height, build, hair, eyes, character and one comparison — and rehearse it aloud. That single prepared paragraph can be adapted to almost any question about a relative, a friend or a famous person.
objectives: Describe physical appearance using adjectives of height, build and colouring
Describe personality and character accurately
Apply the rules of adjective agreement and position
Use comparative forms to compare two people
concepts: Adjectives of appearance (grand, petit, mince, gros, brun, blond)
Adjectives of character (gentil, drôle, sérieux, paresseux, généreux)
Agreement in gender and number (petit/petite/petits/petites)
Adjective position (before or after the noun)
Comparatives (plus ... que, moins ... que, aussi ... que)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: build sentences describing a friend's appearance and personality, choosing the correct forms of the adjectives.

lessons.title: My Home and Neighbourhood
lessons.content:
Housing questions appear in the reading comprehension, in directed situations and in the oral examination. Learn the rooms first: la chambre (bedroom), la cuisine (kitchen), la salle de bains (bathroom), le salon (living room) and le jardin (garden), together with the difference between une maison (a house) and un appartement. French says j'habite dans une maison or simply j'habite une maison; both are heard, and j'habite à ... is followed by the place: J'habite à Kingston.

The structure il y a (there is / there are) is essential for describing a home: Dans ma chambre il y a un lit, une armoire et une petite table. In the negative it becomes il n'y a pas de: Il n'y a pas de garage, but il n'y a pas de voiture means 'there is no car'. Prepositions of place fix the objects: la table est devant la fenêtre, le canapé est à côté de la porte, l'armoire est en face du lit.

Finally, prepare opinions about your area. Use j'aime, je préfère, je n'aime pas and the reason: J'aime mon quartier parce qu'il y a un marché et une belle plage, mais je n'aime pas le bruit. Vocabulary such as le voisin (neighbour), le bruit (noise), calme (quiet), animé (lively), la campagne (countryside) and la ville (town) will help you answer almost any question about where you live.
objectives: Name the rooms and furniture of a house
Describe where you live, using prepositions of place
Say what you like and dislike about your home and area
Use il y a and the negative form correctly
concepts: The house (la maison, l'appartement, la chambre, la cuisine, le salon)
Furniture (le lit, la table, la chaise, l'armoire, le réfrigérateur)
Prepositions of place (devant, derrière, à côté de, en face de, sur, sous)
il y a / il n'y a pas de
Neighbourhood vocabulary (le quartier, le marché, l'église, la plage)

experiment.description: Matching Game: match each room and piece of furniture with the correct French word, then place items in the house using prepositions of place.

lessons.title: School Life, Subjects and Timetable
lessons.content:
School is the first topic many examiners choose, because every candidate has something to say. Learn the buildings and people: le lycée (secondary school), la salle de classe, la bibliothèque, la cantine, le terrain de sport, le professeur and le directeur. Subjects take the definite article: les mathématiques, la physique, la chimie, la biologie, l'histoire, la géographie, l'anglais, le français and l'informatique (computing).

A timetable is described with l'emploi du temps: Le lundi, j'ai les mathématiques de huit heures à dix heures. French uses the 24-hour clock in timetables: dix heures (10.00), dix heures et quart (10.15), dix heures et demie (10.30), quatorze heures (14.00), quinze heures quarante-cinq (15.45). Regular -er verbs follow one pattern: j'étudie, tu étudies, il/elle étudie, nous étudions, vous étudiez, ils/elles étudient. These verbs will carry much of your writing.

For opinions, memorise a structure you can reuse: J'aime l'anglais parce que c'est intéressant, mais je n'aime pas les mathématiques parce que c'est difficile. French says 'the mathematics is difficult' with the singular c'est, and adds pour moi to give an opinion. Adjectives such as utile (useful), ennuyeux (boring), facile (easy) and passionnant (exciting) will let you answer any question about a school subject at length.
objectives: Name school subjects, places and staff in French
Describe your timetable and school day using the 24-hour clock
Talk about what you study and why you like or dislike a subject
Use the present tense of regular -er verbs in a school context
concepts: School places and people (le lycée, la salle de classe, le professeur, le directeur)
Subjects (les mathématiques, la biologie, l'anglais, le français, l'histoire)
Time and the timetable (l'emploi du temps, l'heure, de huit heures à midi)
Present tense of -er verbs (j'étudie, tu étudies, il étudie ...)
Opinions (intéressant, ennuyeux, difficile, utile)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: answer a form teacher's questions about your timetable, subjects and opinions, choosing the right subject vocabulary and time expressions.

lessons.title: Careers, Jobs and the World of Work
lessons.content:
Careers appear in the oral conversation and in directed situations, where you may be asked what you want to do when you leave school. Learn the common professions and note that most now have a feminine form: un professeur / une professeure, un infirmier / une infirmière, un avocat / une avocate, un serveur / une serveuse, un vendeur / une vendeuse, un comptable (same in both). Some, such as un ingénieur / une ingénieure, simply add an -e.

Give reasons with parce que or pour + infinitive: Je voudrais être médecin parce que j'aime aider les gens. Je voudrais travailler dans un hôtel pour rencontrer des touristes. Note that je voudrais (I would like) is the polite conditional, and it is far better examination French than je veux, which sounds abrupt. Mention the qualities the job needs: Il faut être patient et organisé.

Add a second sentence about the training or the workplace: Je devrai étudier la médecine pendant cinq ans à l'université. For those who plan to work in tourism, the Caribbean context gives you ready-made content: le tourisme, un guide touristique, l'aéroport, la réceptionniste. Prepare two or three professions thoroughly, each with a reason, a quality and a training route, and you can answer any careers question.
objectives: Name a range of professions with the correct masculine and feminine forms
Say what job you would like to do and give reasons
Describe what a job involves, using the present tense
Use the conditional form je voudrais politely
concepts: Professions (le médecin, l'infirmier/infirmière, l'avocat, le comptable)
Feminine forms of professions (un instituteur / une institutrice)
Places of work (l'hôpital, le bureau, l'hôtel, l'entreprise)
Je voudrais être ... parce que ...
Skills and qualities (patient, organisé, courageux, bilingue)

experiment.description: Flashcard Trainer: flip cards to learn professions, their feminine forms and the reasons that go with them (je voudrais être ... parce que ...).

lessons.title: Future Plans and Ambitions
lessons.content:
The future tense is examined every year, both in the composition and in the oral conversation. Regular verbs add the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont to the infinitive: je parlerai, tu parleras, elle parlera, nous parlerons. Verbs ending in -re drop the final e: je vendrai. The important irregular stems must be memorised: être becomes ser- (je serai), avoir becomes aur- (j'aurai), aller becomes ir- (j'irai), faire becomes fer- (je ferai), pouvoir becomes pourr- (je pourrai) and venir becomes viendr- (je viendrai).

In everyday speech French often prefers the immediate future, aller + infinitive: Je vais passer mes examens en juin; nous allons visiter la Guadeloupe. Both tenses are acceptable in the examination, but the simple future shows a wider range of language and earns more credit in the composition. Use future time markers to set the scene: l'année prochaine (next year), dans deux ans (in two years), après mes examens (after my exams), un jour (one day), plus tard (later).

A useful pattern for plans that depend on something else is si + present + future: Si je réussis mes examens, j'irai à l'université pour étudier le droit. Si j'obtiens une bourse, je voyagerai en France. Prepare four or five sentences of this kind about your own future — studies, work, travel, family — because they can be adapted to almost any question on the composition paper.
objectives: Form the future tense of regular and common irregular verbs
Express plans and intentions for next year and beyond
Use the immediate future (aller + infinitive) in conversation
Link plans with time expressions for the future
concepts: The simple future (je travaillerai, tu partiras, il finira)
Irregular stems (être - ser-, avoir - aur-, aller - ir-, faire - fer-)
The immediate future (je vais étudier)
Future time markers (l'année prochaine, dans deux ans, un jour)
Si + present, future (Si j'ai de bonnes notes, j'irai à l'université)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: answer a careers adviser's questions about your plans, choosing correctly between the immediate future and the simple future.

lessons.title: Sports and Games
lessons.content:
Sport is a favourite topic in the oral examination because candidates speak about it with enthusiasm. Learn the sports with their articles: le football, le cricket, le basket-ball, le tennis, la natation (swimming), l'athlétisme, le cyclisme and les sports aquatiques. Note that sports ending in -isme and most ball games are masculine, while la natation, la danse and la gymnastique are feminine.

French uses two structures. Jouer à is used for games and team sports: Je joue au football, elle joue au cricket, nous jouons aux cartes (cards). Faire de is used for activities and individual sports: Je fais de la natation, il fait du cyclisme, elles font de l'athlétisme. The contraction matters: à + le = au, à + les = aux; de + le = du, de + les = des. Getting these contractions right is worth marks in every paper.

Add frequency and duration to make your answer sound natural: Je joue au basket deux fois par semaine; je fais de la natation tous les samedis; je ne joue jamais au tennis. Use depuis with the present tense for how long: Je joue au cricket depuis six ans (I have played cricket for six years). Mention a team, a competition or a favourite player, and say why you enjoy the sport — c'est amusant, c'est bon pour la santé, on travaille en équipe — to fill a full examination answer.
objectives: Name a range of sports and sporting equipment in French
Use jouer à and faire de correctly with sports
Talk about a sport you play or watch, and how often
Use depuis and frequency expressions (tous les jours, souvent, parfois)
concepts: Sports (le football, le cricket, le basket, la natation, l'athlétisme)
jouer à + sport versus faire de + sport
Equipment and places (le ballon, le stade, la piscine, le terrain)
Frequency (tous les jours, deux fois par semaine, rarement, jamais)
Depuis + present tense (Je joue au cricket depuis cinq ans)

experiment.description: Flashcard Trainer: flip cards to learn sports with the correct structure — jouer au/à la or faire du/de la.

lessons.title: Leisure Activities and Hobbies
lessons.content:
Leisure is the natural partner of sport in the oral examination: after asking about sport, examiners usually ask what you do in your free time. Learn the vocabulary of hobbies with the right verb: lire un roman (to read a novel), écouter de la musique, regarder un film, jouer aux jeux vidéo, faire de la cuisine, sortir avec des amis, aller à la plage. Opinions follow: J'adore, j'aime beaucoup, je préfère, je n'aime pas du tout, je déteste.

To describe what you did, use the perfect tense. Most verbs take avoir: J'ai regardé un film hier soir; nous avons joué au cricket. A small group of verbs of movement and state take être, and the past participle then agrees with the subject: je suis allé(e), elle est allée, nous sommes resté(e)s, ils sont partis. Memorise the common ones — aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir, rester, monter, descendre, tomber, naître, mourir — and remember the extra -e or -s on the participle.

The imperfect describes what used to happen or sets the scene: Quand j'étais plus jeune, je jouais au football tous les samedis. Mixing the two tenses in one paragraph — Le samedi, je jouais souvent au football, mais le week-end dernier je suis allé au cinéma — is exactly the range of language the examiners reward in Paper 02.
objectives: Name hobbies and leisure activities in French
Describe what you did last weekend using the perfect tense
Distinguish between the perfect and the imperfect for describing past leisure
Express preferences about how you spend free time
concepts: Hobbies (la lecture, la musique, le cinéma, les jeux vidéo, la cuisine)
The perfect tense with avoir (j'ai regardé, j'ai joué)
The perfect tense with être (je suis allé(e), elle est restée)
Agreement of the past participle with être
The imperfect for description (quand j'étais petit, je jouais ...)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: describe your hobbies and last weekend, choosing correctly between the perfect and imperfect tenses.

lessons.title: Healthy Living, Food and Exercise
lessons.content:
Health and healthy living link sports, food and daily routine, and they appear in directed situations where you may be asked to advise a friend. Begin with the food vocabulary: les fruits, les légumes, la viande, le poisson, le riz, le pain, les produits laitiers, les boissons sucrées (sugary drinks). French uses the partitive article for an unspecified quantity: je mange du riz, je bois de l'eau, j'achète des légumes. In the negative it becomes de: je ne mange pas de viande.

To give advice, French uses il faut + infinitive, which is impersonal and very common: Il faut manger plus de légumes et faire de l'exercice; il ne faut pas fumer; il ne faut pas manger trop de sucre. The imperative is also useful and is often asked for directly: Mangez équilibré! Faites du sport trois fois par semaine! Dors au moins huit heures!

Finally, describe your own habits honestly with adverbs of frequency: Je mange des fruits tous les jours, je bois beaucoup d'eau, mais je mange parfois des frites. Use expressions such as en bonne forme (fit), équilibré (balanced), gras (fatty) and sucré (sweet). A short paragraph describing your diet and exercise, with one piece of advice for a friend, answers almost any health question in the oral or written paper.
objectives: Name food and drink groups and say what is healthy
Give advice about diet and exercise using il faut and the imperative
Describe your own habits with adverbs of frequency
Use en and the partitive article (du, de la, des) with food
concepts: Food groups (les fruits, les légumes, la viande, le poisson, les produits laitiers)
The partitive article (du pain, de la salade, des légumes)
Advice (il faut manger, il ne faut pas fumer, faites du sport)
Habits (je mange rarement, je bois beaucoup d'eau)
Health vocabulary (la santé, en bonne forme, le régime, la maladie)

experiment.description: Matching Game: sort foods into healthy and less healthy groups, then match each with advice using il faut and the partitive article.

lessons.title: My Daily Routine and Telling the Time
lessons.content:
A day in the life of a student is one of the most predictable examination topics, so it is worth learning thoroughly. The key verbs are reflexive, because the actions are done to yourself: se lever (to get up), se laver (to wash), se brosser les dents (to brush your teeth), s'habiller (to get dressed), se dépêcher (to hurry) and se coucher (to go to bed). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: je me lève, tu te lèves, il se lève, nous nous levons, vous vous levez, ils se lèvent.

Tell the time with il est: il est six heures (6.00), six heures et quart (6.15), six heures et demie (6.30), sept heures moins le quart (6.45). For anything past the half hour French counts down to the next hour, so 6.45 is 'seven hours minus a quarter'. The 24-hour clock is used for timetables and appointments: le train part à dix-sept heures trente.

Link the events with connectives so that your answer flows: D'abord je me lève à six heures et demie. Ensuite je prends mon petit déjeuner. Puis je vais au lycée en bus. L'après-midi je fais mes devoirs, et enfin je me couche vers dix heures. Notice the useful present-tense verbs that are irregular: prendre (je prends), aller (je vais), faire (je fais) and partir (je pars). Aim for eight to ten sentences in the examination, and put the times in — they prove you can handle numbers as well as verbs.
objectives: Describe a typical school day from morning to night
Use reflexive verbs in the present tense
Tell the time accurately, including the 24-hour clock
Sequence events with time connectives
concepts: Reflexive verbs (se lever, se laver, s'habiller, se coucher)
Reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nous, vous, se)
The time (il est sept heures, sept heures et demie, sept heures et quart)
Time connectives (d'abord, ensuite, puis, après, enfin)
Parts of the day (le matin, l'après-midi, le soir, la nuit)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: answer a pen-friend's questions about your daily routine, building sentences with reflexive verbs and time expressions.

lessons.title: Household Chores and Helping at Home
lessons.content:
Chores connect daily routine with family life, and they are a favourite topic for directed situations. Learn the tasks as whole phrases: faire le lit (to make the bed), faire la vaisselle (to wash up), faire la lessive (to do the washing), passer l'aspirateur (to vacuum), ranger ma chambre (to tidy my room), sortir les poubelles (to take out the rubbish), mettre la table (to lay the table) and préparer le dîner (to cook dinner).

Say how often you do each one: Le samedi matin je fais le lit et je passe l'aspirateur; deux fois par semaine je fais la vaisselle. Obligation is expressed with devoir: Je dois aider ma mère; nous devons ranger la maison avant la visite de mes grands-parents. The stronger, impersonal form il faut + infinitive is also useful: Il faut ranger la cuisine après le repas.

In the perfect tense, most chores are regular: J'ai fait la vaisselle hier soir (note the irregular past participle fait); J'ai rangé ma chambre; j'ai aidé mon père au jardin. For the examination, write about your share of the work and your opinion of it — Je n'aime pas faire la lessive, mais j'aime faire la cuisine — because the examiner is looking for range: chores vocabulary, frequency, obligation and an opinion in one answer. Helping at home also makes a good answer to 'how do you help your parents?', a very common oral question.
objectives: Name household tasks in French
Say what chores you do, how often and when
Use the perfect tense to say what you have done at home
Express obligations with devoir and il faut
concepts: Chores (faire le lit, faire la vaisselle, passer l'aspirateur, ranger)
Frequency and time (le samedi matin, une fois par semaine)
Obligation (je dois, il faut que + subjunctive recognition)
The perfect tense of chores (j'ai fait la vaisselle)
Asking for and giving help (Tu peux m'aider? Bien sûr, je vais t'aider.)

experiment.description: Matching Game: match each chore to its French phrase and to how often it is done, then sort the chores by room.

lessons.title: Weekends, Holidays and Special Days
lessons.content:
Weekend and holiday accounts give you the chance to use several tenses in one answer, which is exactly what the composition paper rewards. Begin with the present: Le samedi matin, je fais les courses avec ma mère; l'après-midi, je retrouve mes amis au terrain de sport. Le dimanche, ma famille va à l'église et nous déjeunons ensemble. Expressions such as en famille, entre amis, faire une promenade and se reposer are all useful here.

For a past holiday, use the perfect tense for the events and the imperfect for the scene: L'année dernière, je suis allé(e) en Guadeloupe avec ma famille. Nous avons pris l'avion à l'aéroport de Kingston. Il faisait très beau et la mer était chaude. Chaque matin nous allions à la plage, et l'après-midi nous visitions les marchés. Note the two tenses working together — this is the single most valuable pattern in Paper 02.

Wrap up with a celebration and an opinion. Le Carnaval de la Martinique, la Fête de la Musique in Guadeloupe and Noël in France all give you something specific to describe: il y avait des défilés, des costumes et de la musique partout; c'était magnifique, mais il y avait beaucoup de monde. Memorise four sequencing words (d'abord, ensuite, puis, enfin) and use them; a clearly ordered account reads as better French than a list of sentences.
objectives: Describe what you do at the weekend using the present tense
Describe a past holiday using the perfect and imperfect
Name festivals and celebrations in the francophone world
Give opinions about a celebration you have attended
concepts: Weekend activities (faire les courses, visiter la famille, aller à l'église)
Past holiday vocabulary (les vacances, la plage, l'hôtel, je suis resté(e))
Festivals (Noël, le Nouvel An, le Carnaval, la Fête de la Musique)
Sequencing in the past (d'abord, puis, le lendemain, enfin)
Opinions (c'était magnifique, j'ai adoré, il y avait beaucoup de monde)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: tell a friend what you did at the weekend and during your last holiday, combining the perfect and imperfect tenses.

lessons.title: Shops, Prices and Quantities
lessons.content:
Shopping is a standard directed situation: you will be asked to write or say what you would say in a shop. Learn the shops and their goods: la boulangerie (bread and cakes), la boucherie (meat), la poissonnerie (fish), la pharmacie, le supermarché, le marché and la boutique de vêtements. A polite request always begins Je voudrais (I would like): Bonjour, je voudrais un pain et deux croissants, s'il vous plaît.

Numbers must be accurate. French counts in a particular way from seventy: soixante-dix (70), soixante et onze (71), quatre-vingts (80), quatre-vingt-dix (90), quatre-vingt-onze (91). Prices use coûter: Combien coûte ce melon? Combien coûtent ces mangues? Note the singular and plural forms. Quantities take de: un kilo de riz, une bouteille d'eau, un paquet de biscuits, une douzaine d'œufs, deux cents grammes de fromage.

Complete the exchange, because the examiner wants the whole situation, not one line: the greeting, the request, the question about price, a comment — C'est trop cher! or C'est raisonnable — and the closing Merci, au revoir. Practise both sides of the conversation: you may be asked what the shopkeeper says as well as what you say.
objectives: Name shops and what they sell
Ask for prices and understand numbers and money in French
Use quantities and containers with de
Hold a simple shopping conversation politely
concepts: Shops (la boulangerie, la boucherie, la pharmacie, le supermarché)
Numbers and money (vingt-cinq, quatre-vingt-dix, un dollar, l'euro)
Quantities (un kilo de, une bouteille de, un paquet de, une douzaine de)
Polite requests (Je voudrais ..., Combien coûte ..., C'est tout?)
Market vocabulary (le marché, les fruits, les légumes, frais)

experiment.description: Flashcard Trainer: flip cards to practise shops, prices and quantity phrases (un kilo de, une bouteille de, une douzaine de).

lessons.title: Clothes, Sizes and Colours
lessons.content:
Clothes vocabulary splits into what is worn on the body and what is worn on the feet, and this helps you remember the gender: la chemise, la robe, la jupe, le pantalon, le maillot de bain (swimwear), les chaussures (f), les sandales (f) and la casquette. The verb porter means to wear: Elle porte une robe bleue et des chaussures noires. Vous êtes habillé(e) en blanc describes a whole outfit.

Colour adjectives agree with the noun and normally follow it: un chemisier blanc, une robe blanche, des chaussures noires, des yeux verts. Four colours are invariant — marron, orange, beige and rose in some usages — and this is a favourite examination trap. Remember also that vert becomes verte, but bleu becomes bleue.

In a clothes shop you need four sentences: Je cherche une chemise (I am looking for a shirt); Quelle est votre taille? (What size are you?); Est-ce que je peux l'essayer? (Can I try it on?); Avez-vous une autre couleur? (Do you have another colour?). Finish with a judgement: C'est trop grand, c'est trop serré (too tight), ça me va bien (it suits me). Practising the shopkeeper's lines as well as your own doubles the usefulness of this lesson in the directed situations section.
objectives: Name clothes and accessories in French
Say colours and understand agreement in colour adjectives
Ask for a different size or colour in a shop
Describe what someone is wearing
concepts: Clothes (la chemise, le pantalon, la robe, les chaussures, la casquette)
Colours (rouge, bleu, vert, blanc, noir, marron, gris)
Sizes and fit (la taille, la pointure, trop grand, trop serré)
Trying on and choosing (je peux l'essayer? dans une autre couleur)
Describing clothes (porter, être habillé en, ça me va bien)

experiment.description: Matching Game: match each garment to its colour and size, paying attention to the agreement of the colour adjectives.

lessons.title: Food Shopping, Meals and the Market
lessons.content:
Food is the most practical shopping topic in the Caribbean examination, because everyone has a market and a favourite dish. Learn the meals first: le petit déjeuner (breakfast), le déjeuner (lunch), le goûter (afternoon snack) and le dîner (dinner). Typical food and drink: le poulet rôti, le poisson frit, le riz et les haricots, les bananes, le jus de fruits, l'eau minérale and la boisson gazeuse.

In a café or restaurant, order politely and completely: Je voudrais un sandwich au poulet et un jus d'orange, s'il vous plaît. You may need to ask for the bill: L'addition, s'il vous plaît. In a market, the useful exchanges are about quantity and quality: C'est combien le kilo de ces tomates? Donnez-moi deux kilos, s'il vous plaît. Ce n'est pas assez mûr. Those fruits are bien frais (nice and fresh) or trop mûrs (overripe).

Finally, be ready to give opinions about food. French uses expressions such as c'est délicieux, c'est épicé (spicy), c'est trop salé (too salty), je préfère le poisson à la viande. Describing a typical meal in your home — what you eat for breakfast and what the family eats on Sunday — is an easy way to show vocabulary, the partitive article (du, de la, des) and an opinion in the same answer.
objectives: Name meals, dishes and drinks in French
Order food in a café or restaurant politely
Shop for food at a market, asking about quantity and quality
Give opinions about food you like and dislike
concepts: Meals (le petit déjeuner, le déjeuner, le goûter, le dîner)
Dishes and drinks (le poulet, le poisson, le riz, le jus, l'eau minérale)
Ordering (Je voudrais, pour moi, l'addition, s'il vous plaît)
Market language (c'est combien le kilo? trop mûr, bien frais)
Opinions (délicieux, trop salé, sucré, épicé)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: complete a market and café conversation, ordering food, asking prices and giving opinions about what you buy.

lessons.title: Transport and Making Travel Arrangements
lessons.content:
Transport is a standard directed situation: buy a ticket, ask for a departure time, or explain how you get to school. Learn the transport and the buildings it uses: le bus (l'arrêt de bus), le train (la gare, le quai), l'avion (l'aéroport), le bateau (le port), le taxi and la voiture. Tickets are bought as un aller simple (one way) or un aller-retour (return).

Prepositions follow a fixed pattern. With transport that you get into, French uses en: en bus, en train, en avion, en voiture, en bateau. With transport that you sit on, it uses à: à vélo, à moto, and for walking à pied. Do not say 'en pied' — a very common error. Ask about times with à quelle heure part le prochain bus pour Montego Bay? and understand the answer at fourteen heures trente, quai numéro deux.

For your own account, explain why you travel the way you do: Je vais au lycée en bus parce que c'est moins cher que le taxi, et le trajet dure vingt minutes. Vocabulary such as le trajet (journey), le billet (ticket), cher (expensive), rapide (fast) and en retard (late) lets you answer any transport question fully. Practise the ticket office exchange in both roles, because the examiner may ask for either.
objectives: Name means of transport and the places they leave from
Buy a ticket and ask about times and platforms
Use en and à with means of transport
Explain how you travel to school and why
concepts: Transport (le bus, le train, l'avion, le bateau, le taxi, la voiture)
Places (la gare, l'aéroport, le port, l'arrêt de bus, le quai)
Buying a ticket (un aller simple, un aller-retour, le prochain départ)
Prepositions (en bus, en voiture, à pied, à vélo)
Times and platforms (à quelle heure, le quai numéro cinq)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: complete a ticket-office conversation — asking for a return ticket, a departure time and the platform — using en and à correctly.

lessons.title: Holidays, Weather and Travelling Abroad
lessons.content:
A holiday account lets you use both past tenses together, which is the strongest single answer you can write. Open with the destination and the transport: L'été dernier, je suis allé(e) à la Martinique avec ma famille; nous avons pris l'avion à Kingston. Then set the scene in the imperfect: Il faisait très beau, il y avait du soleil tous les jours et la mer était chaude.

Weather expressions are the easiest way to build that scene. In the present: il fait beau / mauvais, il fait chaud / froid, il y a du soleil, il pleut, il y a des nuages, il y a du vent. In the past, the imperfect gives il faisait beau and il pleuvait. Link the weather to your plans: Comme il pleuvait, nous sommes restés à l'hôtel; quand il y avait du soleil, nous allions à la plage.

Then narrate what you did, in order: D'abord nous avons visité la ville, ensuite nous avons fait une excursion en bateau, le lendemain nous avons goûté la cuisine locale, finalement nous avons acheté des souvenirs. Finish with a preference and a reason — Je préfère les vacances à la mer parce que je peux nager tous les jours; je n'aime pas la montagne parce qu'il fait froid — so that the account ends with an opinion, which is what the mark scheme rewards.
objectives: Describe past holidays using the perfect and imperfect tenses
Describe the weather in the present and in the past
Say what you did on holiday, in order
Explain your preferences about types of holiday
concepts: Holiday vocabulary (les vacances, séjourner, visiter, se baigner)
The weather (il fait beau, il pleut, il y a du soleil, il fait chaud)
Past weather (il faisait mauvais, il pleuvait)
Ordering events (d'abord, ensuite, le lendemain, finalement)
Preferences (j'aime mieux la mer que la montagne)

experiment.description: Dialogue Builder: describe a past holiday and its weather, choosing correctly between the perfect and the imperfect tenses.

lessons.title: The Francophone World: Countries, Culture and Festivals
lessons.content:
French is spoken by more than three hundred million people, and the francophone world is a favourite theme because it links language to culture. Learn the main countries with their articles: la France, la Belgique, la Suisse, le Canada (le Québec), le Sénégal, la Côte d'Ivoire, la Guadeloupe, la Martinique, la Guyane and Haïti. In the Caribbean, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Guyane and Haïti are all francophone, with a rich créole heritage and their own music: le gwoka in Guadeloupe, le bèlè in Martinique and le compas in Haïti.

Culture questions ask for a description plus an opinion, so prepare one festival and one dish in detail. Le Carnaval, celebrated before Lent, gives you processions, costumes, drums and music; la cuisine créole gives you le colombo, le boudin créole and le gratin de bananes. Use comparatives to compare places: La Martinique est plus petite que la Guadeloupe; le Sénégal est moins industrialisé que la France; Haïti est l'un des pays les plus pauvres de la région. For a superlative, French writes le/la/les plus: la plus grande ville, l'île la plus belle.

Finish with a personal opinion, which is what the oral and composition papers reward: J'aimerais visiter la Guadeloupe parce que la culture créole m'intéresse beaucoup et je pourrais pratiquer mon français tous les jours. A short, factual paragraph of four or five sentences about one francophone country, with a comparison and an opinion, answers any culture question competently.
objectives: Name francophone countries and their capitals
Compare the culture and geography of two francophone places
Describe a francophone festival, dish or custom
Use the comparative and superlative to compare places
concepts: Francophone countries (la France, la Martinique, la Guadeloupe, Haïti, le Sénégal, le Québec)
Continents and nationalities (africain, caribéen, européen, canadien)
Culture (la musique, le carnaval, la cuisine créole, le gwoka, le compas)
Comparatives and superlatives (plus grand que, la plus belle ville)
Travel vocabulary (visiter, découvrir, une région, la population)

experiment.description: Flashcard Trainer: flip cards to learn francophone countries, their capitals and the festivals and dishes that go with them.
